report.query: What evaluation methods exist for LLM reasoning agents?

per_paper_summaries.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: AgentBench provides a benchmark for evaluating LLMs as autonomous agents, highlighting performance gaps and challenges in long-horizon tasks.

per_paper_summaries.title: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: This survey offers a unified framework for LLM-based autonomous agent research, identifying key challenges in the field.

per_paper_summaries.title: ART: Automatic Multi-Step Reasoning and Tool-Use for Large Language Models
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: ART introduces a method for automating multi-step reasoning and tool-use in frozen language models, promoting generalization across tasks.

per_paper_summaries.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: Chain-of-thought prompting enhances LLM reasoning by enabling step-by-step decomposition, significantly improving performance on reasoning benchmarks.

per_paper_summaries.title: Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: RAP demonstrates that using language models as world models with Monte Carlo tree search can improve multi-step reasoning.

overlaps.description: Both papers address the lack of standardized evaluation and conceptual frameworks for LLM-based autonomous agents.
All three papers address the challenge of improving multi-step reasoning in large language models.
Both papers propose methods for enhancing multi-step reasoning in LLMs, with ART focusing on tool use and RAP on planning with a world model.

differences.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
differences.description: AgentBench introduces a comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate LLMs as autonomous agents across multiple environments, focusing on integrated agent behavior rather than isolated capabilities.

differences.title: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents
differences.description: This paper provides a unified conceptual framework for LLM-based autonomous agents and identifies open challenges, offering a broad overview of the field rather than focusing on a specific technical solution.

differences.title: ART: Automatic Multi-Step Reasoning and Tool-Use for Large Language Models
differences.description: ART proposes a novel method for enabling frozen LLMs to perform multi-step reasoning and use external tools without hand-crafted prompts, emphasizing automation and generalization across tasks.

differences.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
differences.description: This paper introduces chain-of-thought prompting, a technique that significantly enhances reasoning performance by encouraging step-by-step decomposition, which becomes effective above a certain model scale.

differences.title: Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
differences.description: RAP treats the language model as a world model for planning, using Monte Carlo tree search to improve multi-step reasoning, highlighting a novel integration of planning and reasoning.

gaps.problem_formulation: The rapid development of LLM-based agents lacks standardized evaluation, and existing benchmarks focus on isolated capabilities rather than integrated agent behavior.
gaps.description: While the problem of lacking standardized evaluation for LLM-based agents is addressed by AgentBench, the method of chain-of-thought prompting, which has been shown to improve reasoning in LLMs, is not applied to this problem. This could potentially enhance the evaluation by incorporating reasoning capabilities into agent behavior assessment.
gaps.supporting_evidence: AgentBench focuses on comprehensive benchmarking but does not mention using chain-of-thought prompting, which is highlighted in the cot_2022 paper as a method to improve reasoning.

gaps.problem_formulation: The lack of a unified conceptual framework for LLM-based autonomous agents and the identification of open challenges in long-term planning, multi-agent coordination, safety, and evaluation methodology.
gaps.description: The survey identifies open challenges in long-term planning and evaluation methodology but does not employ Monte Carlo tree search, a method used in RAP to enhance planning capabilities in LLMs. This method could provide insights into addressing these challenges.
gaps.supporting_evidence: The agentsurvey_2023 paper outlines challenges but does not specify methods like Monte Carlo tree search, which is used in RAP to improve planning.

gaps.problem_formulation: Large language models often fail at multi-step reasoning tasks.
gaps.description: While chain-of-thought prompting addresses multi-step reasoning failures, the use of a comprehensive benchmark like AgentBench could provide a more integrated evaluation of multi-step reasoning capabilities in realistic environments.
gaps.supporting_evidence: cot_2022 focuses on reasoning improvements but does not mention using a benchmark like AgentBench, which evaluates integrated agent behavior.

gaps.problem_formulation: Improving multi-step reasoning by using language models as world models for planning.
gaps.description: RAP uses language models as world models for planning but does not incorporate automatic reasoning and tool-use methods, which could enhance the model's ability to handle complex multi-step tasks.
gaps.supporting_evidence: RAP employs Monte Carlo tree search but does not mention the automatic reasoning and tool-use approach from art_2023, which could complement its planning strategy.

report.synthesis: The analyzed papers collectively highlight the need for rigorous evaluation methods for LLM reasoning agents, emphasizing the challenges in multi-step reasoning and agent task performance. AgentBench and the survey by Wang et al. both address the lack of standardized evaluation, with AgentBench providing a specific benchmark and the survey offering a broad framework for understanding LLM-based agents. Papers like ART and RAP propose innovative methods to enhance reasoning, focusing on tool-use automation and planning with world models, respectively. Meanwhile, chain-of-thought prompting emerges as a crucial technique for improving reasoning capabilities. However, gaps remain in integrating these methods with comprehensive benchmarks and frameworks, which could improve evaluation and planning capabilities in LLM agents.
